advisory.checklist_item: - [ ] Treat epoch=0 (unknown finish age) as WITHIN the grace window (protect it) rather than reapable, or exclude age-unknown rows from the candidate set.
evidence: infra/scripts/container-cap.sh:335-339: `epoch="$(finished_epoch "$finished")"` then `if [ "$epoch" -gt 0 ] && [ $((now - epoch)) -lt "$CONTAINER_MIN_AGE_SECONDS" ]; then ... protected ... continue; fi`
infra/scripts/container-cap.sh:385-386 comment admits: 'an unknown age is treated as reapable only by the sort, never by the grace check.'
infra/scripts/container-cap.sh:368: `$(printf '%s' "$candidates" | sort -n)` sorts epoch=0 rows to the front (reaped first)

Litmus: a Docker engine rendering a FinishedAt format the regex at line 396 misses makes a freshly-exited container immediately reapable — the grace guard's absence is indistinguishable from 'genuinely old enough'.
advisory.finding: In reap(), a container whose FinishedAt timestamp cannot be parsed yields epoch=0, which bypasses the grace-window guard (`[ "$epoch" -gt 0 ] && ...`) and is therefore treated as a reap candidate even if it exited seconds ago. Because candidates are sorted `sort -n` ascending by epoch, epoch=0 rows sort FIRST and are reaped earliest. This contradicts the script's stated grace-window safety guarantee that 'nothing that exited inside CONTAINER_MIN_AGE_SECONDS is ever removed.'
scenarios: A Docker/engine version renders FinishedAt in a format the Python regex does not match, or python3 is unavailable so finished_epoch degrades to 0 for every container.
A container exited 5 seconds ago (operator about to read `docker logs`) but its timestamp is unparseable — it is reaped despite the 900s grace window.
advisory.suggested_fix: Protect age-unknown rows: change the grace check to also skip when epoch<=0, e.g. `if [ "$epoch" -le 0 ] || [ $((now - epoch)) -lt "$CONTAINER_MIN_AGE_SECONDS" ]; then protected_bytes=...; continue; fi`.

advisory.checklist_item: - [ ] Reconcile container_exited_bytes semantics with what the reaper actually reclaims (protected exited containers are excluded), or correct the alarm/runbook so operators do not read df Reclaimable as reaper-reclaimable debris.
evidence: observability.sh:807: `container_exited_bytes          the subset belonging to STOPPED containers, i.e. the debris.`
observability.sh:884: `--metric-name container_exited_bytes --unit Bytes --value "$docker_container_reclaimable"` (sourced from the df Containers `Reclaimable` column, docker_ledger_bytes)

container-cap.sh:331-333: reaper excludes protected containers from candidates — `if protected "$name" "$labels"; then protected_bytes=$((protected_bytes + size)); continue; fi`, so its notion of reclaimable debris is narrower than df Reclaimable

monitoring_autodeploy.tf:740-743: alarm_description says `compare rebar/host:container_exited_bytes against container_writable_bytes to see whether this is reclaimable debris or the live services. REMEDIATION: bash infra/scripts/container-cap.sh --reap forces a pass`
advisory.finding: container_exited_bytes is published from `docker system df` Containers Reclaimable, which counts EVERY stopped container's writable layer, but the reaper deliberately spares compose-labelled and rebar-mcp-* exited containers; the alarm description and runbook nonetheless tell operators to read container_exited_bytes as 'reclaimable debris' and run --reap. The published metric overstates what --reap can actually reclaim, so diagnosis can conclude 'debris' when the bytes are protected crashed services the reaper will never remove.

advisory.checklist_item: - [ ] Replace the verbatim autodeploy.sh source-text assertion in test_the_protected_name_pattern_matches_autodeploys_own_regex with a behavioral check that runs both classifiers over a shared set of container names and asserts identical matched/spared partitions.
evidence: The load-bearing contract is that container-cap.sh's CONTAINER_KEEP_NAME_RE and autodeploy's mcp_managed classify the same container names identically; this is testable by running both classifiers over a shared name set. Pinning autodeploy's implementation text is criterion (a) refactoring violation.
advisory.finding: test_the_protected_name_pattern_matches_autodeploys_own_regex asserts the VERBATIM source text of autodeploy.sh's classifier line rather than the behavioral agreement between the two classifiers; a behavior-preserving refactor of autodeploy.sh (renaming MCP_CONTAINER_PREFIX/MCP_COMPOSE_CONTAINER, switching to egrep, or restructuring the grep) breaks the test with no observable behavior change.
scenarios: autodeploy.sh's mcp-name grep is refactored (variable rename / egrep / multi-line) while preserving which names it matches — the test fails despite no behavior change.

advisory.checklist_item: - [ ] Add a container-cap.sh reap test with finished='0001-01-01T00:00:00.000000000Z' asserting the never-started zero-timestamp container is classified per the documented age-unknown/grace behavior.
evidence: Added code: finished_epoch prints max(epoch,0) and its comment states 'A container that never ran carries the zero timestamp 0001-01-01T00:00:00Z ... Reported as 0 = age unknown, which the grace check below treats as NOT recently finished'
search_files for '0001' in tests/scripts/test_container_cap.py returned (no matches) — no test drives finished='0001-01-01T00:00:00.000000000Z'
The reap tests use finished defaults of 2000-01-01 (past) and 2999-01-01 (future) only, so the epoch-0/never-started branch is never exercised.
advisory.finding: container-cap.sh's newly-added finished_epoch special-cases the never-started zero timestamp 0001-01-01T00:00:00Z (returns 0 = 'age unknown', treated as NOT recently-finished by the grace check yet reapable by the sort), but no test in test_container_cap.py exercises a container carrying that timestamp.
scenarios: An exited-but-never-run container (docker create without start) is present and over-share: the epoch-0 path decides whether it is reaped; a regression that mishandled it (e.g. treating epoch 0 as within the grace window, or the negative-epoch clamp regressing) would go undetected.

dropped.checklist_item: - [ ] Reconcile docs/comments with census(): either add `--filter status=exited --filter status=dead` to the `docker ps -a` call, or correct the header/runbook/comments to describe the actual shell-classification + no-force-rm guarantee.
evidence: infra/scripts/container-cap.sh:275-276: `ids="$(_docker ps -a --format '{{.ID}}' 2>/dev/null)"` — no `--filter status=` at all
infra/scripts/container-cap.sh:115-117 comment: 'candidates come from `--filter status=exited --filter status=dead`, which never lists a running container'
infra/scripts/container-cap.sh:57-61 header and runbook (infra/runbooks/review-bot-ops.md) repeat the same `--filter status=exited --filter status=dead` claim
Actual running-exclusion is at infra/scripts/container-cap.sh:326-330 (shell `if [ "$status" = "running" ]` / `case ... exited|dead`)
dropped.finding: The header, usage docs, runbook, and inline comments repeatedly assert that candidates come from `docker ps -a --filter status=exited --filter status=dead`, 'which never lists a running container' — presenting this as a daemon-enforced guarantee. But census() actually runs `docker ps -a` with NO status filter and then classifies running/exited/dead in shell. The claimed daemon-level filter that 'never lists a running container' is not what the code does; the running-container exclusion rests entirely on the shell status branch plus the `docker rm` (no -f) refusal, not on the advertised filter.
scenarios: A maintainer trusts the header's daemon-filter claim and later refactors classify() away, believing the daemon guarantees running exclusion.
Reviewer auditing the safety argument cannot find the filter the docs cite because it does not exist in census().
dropped.suggested_fix: Add the documented filters to the census listing (`docker ps -a --filter status=exited --filter status=dead --format '{{.ID}}'`) so the code matches the asserted guarantee — but note census also uses .SizeRw of running containers for container_writable_bytes context; if the full set is needed, correct the prose instead.
